rationale: A wins because it knows where the bodies are buried and refuses to connect facts the update does not connect. Its line, "Is the manufacturer using the on-device model, or only the hosted tier?" is exactly the question B fails to ask before writing "Offline AI That Runs on a Laptop Is Now Good Enough for a Fortune 100 Factory." B has usable bones, but two of its loudest angles are built on an invented bridge between the manufacturer and offline deployment.
gaps_in_A: "A Fortune 100 manufacturer is paying Hugging Face to keep its models private" is a shade too certain; the update says a Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early enterprise customer, not that privacy is its stated reason for buying.
"The prevailing belief is that reasoning quality tracks parameter count" imports outside beat context. Plausible, but source it or soften it before pitching.
"at least one developer or app using it offline" is correctly listed as proof, but that also means the developer-adoption angle is not pitch-ready from the supplied facts alone.
gaps_in_B: "Offline AI That Runs on a Laptop Is Now Good Enough for a Fortune 100 Factory" invents the core story. The update does not say the manufacturer uses the on-device model, runs it in a factory, or has proven it is good enough for real workloads.

"The Factory That Runs AI Without a Cloud Connection" is the same invented leap in a tighter headline. No cloud connection, plant-floor use, data sovereignty reason, or operational use case was supplied.
"a Fortune 100 manufacturer already using it" turns an early enterprise hub customer into proof of on-device model adoption. That is how a pitch dies on the first fact-check call.

"no per-query costs, no data leaving the network, and no contract to renegotiate when pricing changes" overextends the Apache 2.0/offline facts into procurement and architecture claims the update does not support.
